notes: Analyst pass. (1) The baseline is strong — this model writes good ETL unaided, so the headline delta (100% vs 95%) understates the qualitative gap; the differences live in *contract*, not capability. (2) The one baseline failure is the archetypal one: eval-0 baseline PADDED the ragged row into the output (inventing a value) and its machine-readable report omits that row entirely — prose notes were honest, telemetry was not. The skill quarantined the same row with a coded error record (STR-02). (3) Non-assertion divergences worth noticing: eval-0 baseline silently DROPPED the exact-duplicate row (taxonomy default is keep-and-report; a repeated order is destroyed); it also auto-repaired mojibake by default, where the skill treats repair as opt-in (flagged ENC-06). Neither was asserted — candidate assertions for iteration 2. (4) Eval-1 assertions did not discriminate (7/7 both): the never-guess-dates behavior is model-innate here. The real difference is disposition: skill quarantined ambiguous-date rows for reprocessing; baseline loaded them with NULL dates + annotation — different downstream semantics, same 'didn't guess' credit. Consider a sharper assertion about reprocessability. (5) Eval-2 shows the composability payoff: with-skill was FASTER (85s vs 145s) and equal-token, because regeneration from a spec over a known runtime is mostly mechanical. The skill's cost (+123s, +33k tokens mean) concentrates in evals 0-1 where it runs profiling + spec authoring — that overhead buys the spec artifact and uniform report contract, which the assertions only partially price in. (6) Assertions that always pass regardless of skill (runs-to-completion, report-exists) are non-discriminating filler — replace with contract-level checks (machine-readable accounting completeness, duplicate policy, quarantine reprocessability) next iteration.
